full_title: CORPUS B. ALZATE, COMPLAINANT, VS. HON. RAPHIEL F. ALZATE, PRESIDING JUDGE, BRANCH 1, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, BANGUED, ABRA, RESPONDENT.
docket: A.M. No. RTJ-25-099 [Formerly OCA IPI No. 18-4879-RTJ]
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 1. Standards of Ethical Conduct of Judges and Justices > d. Impartiality (Canon III) > i. Mandatory vs. Voluntary Inhibition (See also Rule 137)
topics: Compulsory inhibition where the judge's spouse acted as counsel in the case
Spouse-counsel's withdrawal does not remove the ground for inhibition
Violating the rule on compulsory disqualification is gross ignorance of the law or procedure
Substantial evidence in administrative cases against judges; gross misconduct and dishonesty not proved
Penalty when the respondent judge has already been dismissed; disbarment prayer

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)

doctrine:
**A judge must inhibit from a case in which his spouse acted as counsel. Under Rule 137, Section 1 of the Rules of Court and Canon III, Section 5 and Canon IV, Section 4 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, the inhibition is "not merely discretionary; it is compulsory."** Canon IV, Section 4 provides that judges "shall not participate in the determination of a case in which any member of their family represents a litigant or is associated in any manner with the case." **The spouse's withdrawal as counsel when the judge took over the case does not cure the disqualification.** She had actively participated before withdrawing (she prepared and filed the petition and presented the petitioner's evidence-in-chief), so a perception that the case was decided in her favor remains. A judge should not handle a case where there is a perception, rightly or wrongly, that he is susceptible to bias because of relationship.

**Disobeying the rule on compulsory self-disqualification is gross ignorance of the law or procedure** (following *Paderanga v. Judge Paderanga*), not simple misconduct as the JIB had recommended. It is a serious charge under Rule 140, as amended, punishable by dismissal, suspension of more than six months to one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000.00 up to PHP 200,000.00.

In administrative cases, the complainant must prove the allegations by **substantial evidence**. Mere allegations, conjectures and suppositions, such as a court's reputation as the "Annulment Capital of the North" or a "conjugal syndicate" offering "package deals," do not establish gross misconduct (which requires corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules) or dishonesty (reiterated).
facts:
Complainant Judge Corpus Alzate charged respondent Judge Raphiel F. Alzate with misconduct and dishonesty in annulment cases in Branch 58, RTC, Bucay, Abra, which respondent presided over. He alleged that the branch was known as the "Annulment Capital of the North" and disregarded the residency requirement. He also alleged that respondent and his wife, Atty. Maria Saniata Liwliwa Gonzales-Alzate, were a "conjugal syndicate" offering "package deals": the wife would deal with the parties and assign the case to "accommodating" lawyers who did not take part in the proceedings, and respondent would decide in the parties' favor.

He cited two nullity cases. In *Villanueva v. Villanueva* (Civil Case No. 13-764), filed on June 24, 2013 when Judge Dojillo still presided, Atty. Gonzales-Alzate was counsel of record. She prepared the petition and presented the petitioner, Villanueva, to testify before Judge Dojillo. Complainant alleged that Villanueva, respondent's childhood best friend, actually lived in Bangued and not Bucay. Respondent was designated acting presiding judge on September 2, 2013. His wife then moved to withdraw as counsel, and respondent granted the motion at a November 7, 2013 hearing. He then tried and decided the case without inhibiting. Minutes of a March 2014 hearing bore the wife's name, which the court interpreter certified was his own inadvertence. In *Bermudez v. Bermudez* (Civil Case No. 14-804), complainant alleged that counsel of record Atty. Byrone Alzate merely lent his name, was never notified of hearings, and that the petition was granted without witnesses or a hearing. Atty. Byrone Alzate gave two contradictory affidavits. Respondent submitted affidavits and barangay certifications that both petitioners resided in Bucay.

Complainant asked that respondent be held liable and that the case also be treated as a disbarment proceeding. The Investigating Justice of the Court of Appeals found the evidence of gross misconduct and dishonesty insufficient. He treated non-inhibition in *Villanueva* as a matter of voluntary inhibition and recommended a judicial audit. The Office of the Executive Director of the Judicial Integrity Board (JIB) found that respondent violated Rule 137, Section 1 and the New Code of Judicial Conduct by not inhibiting, and recommended a PHP 5,000.00 fine. The JIB found him guilty of simple misconduct and, citing his prior administrative liabilities, recommended a PHP 100,000.00 fine.
issues: Whether respondent is guilty of gross misconduct and dishonesty in deciding the Villanueva and Bermudez nullity cases and through the alleged "package deals."
Whether respondent is administratively liable for not inhibiting from Villanueva, in which his wife had been counsel, and for what offense.
What penalty should be imposed, and whether the case should also be treated as a disbarment proceeding.
ruling:
**1. No. Gross misconduct and dishonesty were not proved.** The complainant must prove the charges by substantial evidence; "mere allegation is not equivalent to proof." Gross misconduct is a serious transgression of an established rule that threatens the administration of justice, manifested in corruption or acts "done with the clear intent to violate the law or in flagrant disregard of established rules." The Court adopted the JIB's findings. No substantial evidence showed that respondent and his wife negotiated "package deals." The non-residency allegations were "sufficiently disputed" by affidavits and certifications. Neither the non-inhibition in *Villanueva* nor the claim that Atty. Byrone Alzate was never notified in *Bermudez* showed corruption. The Court noted that respondent's handling of nullity cases had already been examined in an audit case (*In re Alzate*), where he was found guilty of gross neglect of duty for proceeding without pre-trial and without awaiting collusion reports.

**2. Yes. Respondent is guilty of gross ignorance of the law or procedure for failing to inhibit in *Villanueva*.** Respondent did not deny that his wife filed the petition, and he admitted that she presented the petitioner to testify before Judge Dojillo. Under Rule 137, Section 1, Canon III, Section 5 and Canon IV, Section 4 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, "respondent's inhibition in Villanueva is not merely discretionary; it is compulsory. There is no excuse for respondent's failure to inhibit in said case." His defense that his wife had withdrawn failed: "such withdrawal does not change the fact that respondent's wife actively participated in the said case prior to her withdrawal," and a perception remains that the case was decided in her favor. A judge must not only be impartial but must also appear impartial. **Following *Paderanga*, the rules on compulsory self-disqualification are "as basic as a rule of thumb," so disobeying them is gross ignorance of the law or procedure, not the simple misconduct the JIB found.**

**3. A fine of PHP 200,000.00; no disbarment in this case.** Gross ignorance of the law or procedure is a serious charge under Rule 140, as amended, punishable by dismissal, suspension of more than six months to one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000.00 but not exceeding PHP 200,000.00. In *Sindon v. Alzate*, respondent had been reprimanded and warned for not inhibiting in his wife's application for a notarial commission. In the audit case he was suspended for five years for gross neglect of duty, and he was later dismissed from the service for failing to comply with the Court's directive there. This was his second violation of the rule on compulsory disqualification and his third administrative liability, and he had already been dismissed. The Court therefore imposed a fine of PHP 200,000.00. On the disbarment prayer, the Court found that "the offense respondent is guilty of in this case does not affect his qualification as a lawyer" and penalized him only as a member of the bench. It nonetheless directed the JIB to report on his fitness to remain a member of the Bar.
disposition: Judge Raphiel F. Alzate was found GUILTY of Gross Ignorance of the Law and ORDERED to pay a fine of PHP 200,000.00 within 30 days from finality, and to submit proof of payment within 10 days from payment. Failure to comply would lead to contempt proceedings under Rule 71, Section 3. Copies were ordered furnished to the Office of the Bar Confidant, the OCA's Office of Administrative Services (for his personal file), the OCA (for dissemination to all courts), and the Integrated Bar of the Philippines. The Judicial Integrity Board was directed to prepare a comprehensive report and recommendation on his fitness to remain a member of the Bar.

bar_questions.q: Atty. Lorna filed a petition for declaration of nullity of marriage for her client and presented him as a witness on direct examination before Judge Santos. Judge Santos was later transferred, and Judge Mario, Atty. Lorna's husband, was designated acting presiding judge of the branch. Atty. Lorna immediately moved to withdraw as counsel, and Judge Mario granted the motion. He then tried the rest of the case and granted the petition, reasoning that his wife was no longer counsel of record. (a) Was Judge Mario required to inhibit? (b) What is his administrative liability?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. His inhibition was compulsory, and his wife's withdrawal did not cure the disqualification. (b) He is liable for gross ignorance of the law or procedure, a serious charge.
alac.legal_basis: Rule 137, Section 1 of the Rules of Court and Canon III, Section 5 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct require judges to disqualify themselves where it may appear to a reasonable observer that they cannot decide impartially. Canon IV, Section 4 provides that judges shall not participate in the determination of a case in which any member of their family represents a litigant or is associated in any manner with the case. In Alzate v. Judge Alzate (A.M. No. RTJ-25-099, August 5, 2025, En Banc), the Court held that a judge's inhibition from a case in which his wife had been counsel was "not merely discretionary; it is compulsory." Her withdrawal did not change the fact that she actively participated before withdrawing. Disobeying the rule on compulsory self-disqualification is gross ignorance of the law or procedure, a serious charge under Rule 140, as amended.
alac.application: Atty. Lorna prepared and filed the petition and presented the petitioner's testimony, so she was associated with the case. Her withdrawal when her husband took over left intact the perception that the case would be, and was, decided in her favor. Judge Mario's belief that he could sit because she was no longer counsel of record is exactly the defense the Court rejected in Alzate. Because the rules on compulsory disqualification are basic, his failure to observe them is gross ignorance of the law or procedure, not mere simple misconduct.
alac.conclusion: Judge Mario should have inhibited, and he is administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law or procedure.

bar_questions.q: A complaint against Judge Ramos alleged that his branch had become known among lawyers as the "Annulment Capital" of the region, that he and his lawyer-wife offered "package deals" to couples, and that he granted nullity petitions of parties who did not reside in his territorial jurisdiction. The complainant offered only his own allegations and the reputation of the court. Judge Ramos submitted affidavits of the petitioners' relatives and barangay certifications showing that the petitioners resided within his territory. Should Judge Ramos be held liable for gross misconduct and dishonesty?

alac.answer: No. The charges of gross misconduct and dishonesty are not supported by substantial evidence.
alac.legal_basis: In administrative proceedings, the complainant has the burden of proving the allegations by substantial evidence, or such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion. Mere allegations, conjectures and suppositions cannot be given credence. Gross misconduct requires a serious transgression of an established rule, manifested in corruption or acts done with clear intent to violate the law or in flagrant disregard of established rules. Dishonesty is a disposition to lie, cheat, deceive or defraud. (Alzate v. Judge Alzate, A.M. No. RTJ-25-099, August 5, 2025, En Banc, citing Zara v. Joyas)
alac.application: The complainant relied on reputation and his own assertions; he presented no competent evidence of any "package deal" or corrupt arrangement. The residency allegations were rebutted by affidavits and barangay certifications. As in Alzate, where identical charges were dismissed for lack of substantial evidence, nothing in the record shows corruption or a clear intent to violate the law.
alac.conclusion: Judge Ramos cannot be held liable for gross misconduct and dishonesty on the basis of unproven allegations and reputation.

bar_questions.q: Judge Cruz was found to have violated the rule on compulsory inhibition. Years earlier, he had been reprimanded with a warning for the same kind of violation. In another case, he was suspended for gross neglect of duty and later dismissed from the service. (a) Given that he has already been dismissed, what penalty may still be imposed for his gross ignorance of the law or procedure? (b) The complainant asks the Court to disbar Judge Cruz in the same administrative case. Must the Court do so?

alac.answer: (a) A fine; the Court may impose the maximum fine of PHP 200,000.00 for a serious charge. (b) No. Where the offense does not affect his qualification as a lawyer, the Court may penalize him only as a member of the bench.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court, as amended, gross ignorance of the law or procedure is a serious charge punishable by dismissal from the service, suspension of more than six months but not exceeding one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000.00 but not exceeding PHP 200,000.00. In Alzate v. Judge Alzate (A.M. No. RTJ-25-099, August 5, 2025, En Banc), the Court imposed a PHP 200,000.00 fine on a judge who had already been dismissed from the service. It considered that this was his second violation of the rule on compulsory disqualification and his third administrative liability. The Court declined to treat the case as a disbarment proceeding because the offense did not affect his qualification as a lawyer, but directed the JIB to report on his fitness to remain a member of the Bar.
alac.application: (a) Dismissal and suspension are no longer possible because Judge Cruz is out of the service, but a fine can still be imposed. His prior reprimand for the same kind of violation and his other administrative liability justify the maximum fine of PHP 200,000.00, as in Alzate. (b) A judge's failure to inhibit is an offense committed as a member of the bench. If it does not affect his qualification as a lawyer, the Court may confine the penalty to his judicial accountability. It may separately look into his fitness as a lawyer, as it did in Alzate by directing a JIB report.
alac.conclusion: Judge Cruz may be fined PHP 200,000.00, and the Court is not required to disbar him in the same case, though it may separately examine his fitness to remain a lawyer.

notes: The decision applied Rule 137, the New Code of Judicial Conduct (A.M. No. 03-05-01-SC) and Rule 140, as amended. The 2027 syllabus is based on the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC), which the decision does not mention; the syllabus heading is the closest match. The complaint dates the wife's withdrawal to November 4, 2013, while respondent says the motion was granted at the November 7, 2013 hearing. The caption names respondent as Presiding Judge, Branch 1, RTC Bangued, Abra, but the acts complained of were in Branch 58, RTC Bucay, Abra, and the JIB called him a "former" presiding judge. The fallo says "Gross Ignorance of the Law," while the body says "gross ignorance of the law or procedure."
